content.title: About
content.content: Cheddar is a hard cheese with a distinctive sharp flavor, originating from the English county of Somerset. It is made from cow’s milk and aged from several months to several years, which determines its intensity of taste and color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cheddar was produced in the 12th century in the village of Cheddar, giving the cheese its name.
Mature cheddar can be aged up to 10 years, developing a crystalline texture and a more pronounced aroma.
The cheese’s orange hue is often enhanced with annatto, a natural pigment derived from the seeds of the achiote tree.
Cheddar is widely used in melt‑friendly dishes such as macaroni and cheese and cheeseburgers.
In the United States, cheddar is one of the most consumed cheeses.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheddar provides a high amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: During aging, beneficial bacteria develop, which can promote gut health.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Cheddar includes vitamins A and D, important for vision and immune function.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or lactose may experience reactions when consuming cheddar.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Cheddar contains a notable amount of saturated fats, so it should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: The cheese is often salty; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheddar is calorie‑dense, and large servings can contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheddar can be enjoyed sliced, grated into salads, soups, and casseroles, or used in hot dishes where it melts. Choose a younger cheddar for a milder taste and an aged cheddar for a sharper flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cheddar in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage, wrap it in wax paper followed by aluminum foil to prevent drying out. Use the cheese within 3‑4 weeks after opening.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg omelet and scrambled egg are classic egg dishes that have been on fast‑food and restaurant menus since 1979. Eggs are beaten (for an omelet) or cracked directly onto a hot pan (for scrambled eggs), a small amount of oil or butter is added, and they are cooked to the desired doneness. The result is a tender, mildly flavored protein‑rich dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the oldest foods consumed by humans, with a history of over 6,000 years.
In 1979 many fast‑food chains introduced omelets as a "healthier" alternative to processed meats.
The Japanese rolled omelet, tamagoyaki, is a sweet, layered specialty.
There are countless variations: cheese, vegetables, ham, mushrooms, and even seafood can be added.
Eggs are one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A large egg provides about 6‑7 g of complete protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Eggs contain B12, riboflavin and folate, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of choline
items.content: Choline supports liver function and brain health, including memory.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Omelets and scrambled eggs contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk help protect eye health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Risk of salmonella
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor salmonella; it is recommended to cook until the whites are fully set.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: The yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should moderate yolk intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Adding butter, cheese, or meat can significantly increase the calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Omelets are served hot, often folded or rolled, with fillings such as cheese, vegetables, ham or mushrooms. Scrambled eggs are cooked gently, sometimes with milk or cream for a softer texture, and can be eaten alone or as part of a breakfast sandwich or burger.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw eggs in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in their original carton. Cooked omelet or scrambled eggs should be eaten within 2 hours, or kept in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 24 hours. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before consumption.

mushrooms-fresh-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-t.title: Mushrooms, fresh, cooked, fat added, NS as to fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Mushrooms are edible fruiting bodies of fungi that can be eaten fresh or after cooking. When prepared with added fat (oil, butter, or other fats) they develop a richer flavor and texture, and their caloric value increases. The specific type of fat is not specified (NS).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushrooms are the only non‑animal source of complete protein, though the amount is lower than in legumes.
Vitamin D content rises dramatically after exposure to ultraviolet light.
Mushrooms can accumulate certain heavy metals from the soil.
In culinary practice, fat is often used to enhance flavor and improve texture of mushrooms.
There are over 10,000 edible mushroom species, but only a small fraction is commercially available.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms provide niacin, riboflavin, pyridoxine and folate, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Without added fat, 100 g of fresh mushrooms contain about 22 kcal, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in mushrooms aids regular bowel movements and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Ergothioneine and glutathione in mushrooms help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Beta‑glucans stimulate immune cells and may enhance the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to certain mushroom varieties.

items.title: Toxic look‑alikes
items.content: Edible mushrooms can be confused with poisonous ones, so purchase only from reputable sources.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Mushrooms contain purines, which may be a concern for people with gout.

items.title: Increased calories with fat
items.content: Adding fat raises the dish’s energy density, which should be considered in calorie counting.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mushrooms can be eaten raw in salads, but are most often sautéed, stir‑fried, baked, or boiled. When cooking with added fat, use vegetable oils or butter in moderate amounts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh mushrooms in a paper bag in the refrigerator for 1–3 days. Cooked mushrooms with added fat should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2 days.
